To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the methods of dealing with missing data in meta-analysesshould be reported in a transparent and consistent manner, and the impact of different missing data assumptions on meta-analytical pooled effect estimates should be assessed in order to test the robustnessthereof.

we found that the impact of different assumptions for missing participant data (i.e. imputing the outcome data for missing participants) on the pooled effect estimate of meta-analysis is substantial, and that there is no consensus on which categories of trial patients should be considered as having missing outcome data.
The impact of different assumptions about missing participant data (e.g. missing at random) on pooled effect estimates was small and not clinically relevant.

a meta-analysis of dichotomised outcomes should not be based on trials with missing data, and if this is not possible, the authors should report the results of the analysis using several methods to deal with MPD, and discuss the implications.
the methodological approach used in the systematic review is appropriate, given the available data.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
systematic reviews should report on how they dealt with MPD.
we will provide recommendations for the reporting of systematic reviews with MPD.

we assess how trial participants are defined as having MPD, how trialists reported MPD, what systematic reviewers report doing, what systematic reviewers actually do when dealing with MPD, and the impact on pooled effect estimates of different methods of imputing MPD.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the methods for dealing with MPD should be reported clearly, and that authors conducting meta-analysis of dichotomised outcomes should consider the potential impact of their choice of method for dealing with MPDs on the results of their meta-analysis.
systematic reviewers should report on how they deal with MPD in the meta-analytical process, and that they should use a consistent method for each outcome of interest.
we need more information on MPD in systematic reviews and in trials, and more transparency regarding what authors of systematic reviews actually did in their meta-analytical procedures.
